scenarios.title: Where does this alert belong?
scenarios.why: Tier 1 owns monitoring, triage, initial evidence gathering, and playbook-driven containment, then escalates with complete notes. Attribution, rule rewrites, and infrastructure-wide outages belong to higher tiers or engineering. Escalating with rich context is a feature of good Tier 1 work, not a failure.

Follow the playbook: verify the sign-in context (user travel, VPN egress, session details) before acting
Call the user at 2 AM to ask if they logged in
Mark the alert as a false positive because the password was correct

scenarios.hint: Why would an organization write the verification steps down instead of trusting analyst instinct?

scenarios.situation: An alert fires at 02:14: 'Multiple failed logins followed by a successful login from an unusual country.' You open the playbook for 'impossible travel / anomalous login.'
scenarios.title: The alert at 2 AM
scenarios.why: Playbooks exist so the 2 AM analyst makes the same disciplined decision as the noon analyst. Verifying context first avoids locking out a traveling executive or missing a real compromise. Disabling first is sometimes right, but only after the playbook's verification steps say so — context determines whether containment or clearance is next.

choices: Close the ticket so the queue looks clean; the next shift will see the isolated host
Leave it open with no notes — the evidence speaks for itself in the SIEM
Write a concise handoff note: what you know, what you did, what is unconfirmed, and recommended next steps
Reverse the isolation so the next analyst starts from a clean state
evidence: Review the relevant soc-workflow documentation.
scenarios.hint: If you were the incoming analyst, what four things would you need to pick this up cold?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best handoff practice?
scenarios.situation: Your shift ends in 20 minutes. You are mid-investigation on a suspicious PowerShell alert; you have isolated the host but have not yet confirmed maliciousness. The next analyst just logged in.
scenarios.title: The handoff gap
scenarios.why: SOC continuity lives in handoff notes. 'Known / done / unconfirmed / next' lets the incoming analyst continue in minutes instead of re-doing hours of work. Closing tickets to look clean hides risk; reversing containment destroys your defensive posture for aesthetics.

The metric is being gamed — speed without evidence quality means detections may be missed
MTTR is irrelevant and should be replaced entirely by headcount
Bulk-closing is fine because most alerts are false positives anyway

scenarios.hint: What behavior does a pure speed metric reward, and what does it punish?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most accurate interpretation?
scenarios.situation: Leadership celebrates that mean time to respond (MTTR) dropped 40% this quarter. You notice analysts are bulk-closing alerts with 'no malicious activity found' and no evidence attached.
scenarios.title: What MTTR hides
scenarios.why: Metrics drive behavior. MTTR that rewards closing speed incentivizes shallow triage. Healthy SOC metrics pair speed with quality measures: escalation accuracy, evidence completeness, and reopen rates. A falling MTTR alongside falling evidence quality is a red flag, not a win.

choices: Treat it as a security incident and isolate the switch from the network
Triage it as an availability issue, rule out malicious cause quickly, and hand off to the NOC/network team with findings
Ignore it — hardware failures are never the SOC's problem
Open a full incident and page the CISO

scenarios.hint: What's the SOC's job here — fixing the switch, or answering one specific question about it?

scenarios.situation: A core switch is flapping, causing intermittent outages across two floors. The ticket lands in the SOC queue because 'network anomaly' matched a detection rule.
scenarios.title: SOC or NOC?
scenarios.why: The SOC triages everything in its queue but does not own everything. A quick malicious-cause check (is the flapping consistent with an attack, or with hardware failure?) followed by a clean handoff to the NOC respects both missions. Ignoring it risks missing an attack disguised as failure; owning it wastes the SOC's incident capacity.

The playbook defines the overall response strategy and decision points; the runbook gives the step-by-step clicks and commands to execute it
The runbook is for managers; the playbook is for analysts
Playbooks are only used after an incident is declared closed

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct distinction?
scenarios.situation: Your SOC has both runbooks and playbooks for phishing. A new analyst asks when to use which during an active phish with a malicious attachment.
scenarios.title: Runbook vs playbook
scenarios.why: A playbook answers 'what is our strategy and when do we escalate'; a runbook answers 'exactly which console, which query, which button, in what order.' Both are needed: strategy without steps is slow, steps without strategy are blind. New analysts should reach for the runbook for execution and the playbook for judgment calls.

scenarios.title: SOC Workflow: Design Decision
scenarios.situation: You need to make an architecture/design decision for SOC Workflow in a Soc Analyst environment. Multiple approaches are viable, but each has tradeoffs.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach best balances the competing concerns for this SOC Workflow scenario?
choices: Analyze the requirements, evaluate each option against constraints (performance, cost, complexity, maintainability), select the approach with the best tradeoff profile, and document the decision rationale including rejected alternatives.
Choose the most familiar approach — comfort matters more than fit.
Choose the newest technology — latest is always best.
Delay the decision — more analysis is always better.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Architecture decisions require structured evaluation: (1) Clarify requirements and constraints, (2) Enumerate viable options, (3) Score each against weighted criteria, (4) Select the best tradeoff, (5) Document why others were rejected. This prevents both analysis paralysis and reckless choices in SOC Workflow design.
scenarios.hint: Think about how senior engineers make decisions — it's not gut feel, it's structured evaluation.

Apply the most common solution immediately without analysis.
Defer to someone else — this is too complex.
Try random approaches until something works.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Expert SOC Workflow work in Soc Analyst requires: systematic analysis (understand all factors), prioritization (impact × urgency), verified implementation (check each step), and documentation (team learning). This disciplined approach distinguishes senior practitioners.

Normal backup activity — service accounts retry often
A misconfigured monitoring script — ask the backup team to fix the retries
A brute-force attack that failed — no success means no incident

02:11:03 sshd[4412]: Failed password for svc-backup from 203.0.113.77 port 51230
02:11:04 sshd[4412]: Failed password for svc-backup from 203.0.113.77 port 51231
... (412 similar lines) ...

scenarios.hint: Which single log line changes this from an attempt into a suspected success?
scenarios.prompt: What does this pattern most likely indicate, and what is your next step?
scenarios.situation: You pull authentication logs for a service account after an alert. The last hour shows hundreds of failed logins from one external IP, then silence.
scenarios.title: The login wall
scenarios.why: Hundreds of failures from a single IP followed by an 'Accepted' is the classic brute-force-success signature. The silence after success is the attacker switching to quiet post-exploitation behavior. The accepted login is the line that converts this from 'attempt' to 'likely compromise' — escalate with the full timeline attached.

choices: DNS tunneling / data exfiltration — confirm by checking query entropy, response sizes, and whether the host should contact that domain
A browser misconfiguration — clear the DNS cache and move on
Normal CDN behavior — CDNs use many subdomains
A DNS server outage — the retries explain the volume

scenarios.hint: What is being carried inside those subdomain labels, and why would they all be unique?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest hypothesis, and what evidence confirms it?
scenarios.situation: A workstation is generating thousands of DNS queries to a strange subdomain pattern under an unfamiliar domain. Query volume is 50x the host's baseline.
scenarios.title: Chatty DNS
scenarios.why: High-entropy, unique subdomains at high volume to an unfamiliar domain is the textbook DNS tunneling/exfil pattern — data is encoded in the subdomain labels. Confirm with entropy analysis, NXDOMAIN/response patterns, and baseline comparison. CDNs do use many subdomains, but not high-entropy random labels at 50x baseline from one host.

Kill PowerShell and close the ticket — the EDR already blocked it
Uninstall PowerShell from the workstation to prevent recurrence
Email the user asking if they ran a macro

scenarios.prompt: What is your best next step as the triaging analyst?

scenarios.title: The encoded command
scenarios.why: Winword spawning hidden, encoded PowerShell is one of the highest-fidelity malicious indicators in endpoint telemetry — it is the classic malicious-macro chain. Decode safely (offline/sandbox, never on a production box), preserve volatile state, and escalate with the decoded intent. Killing the process without understanding intent destroys evidence of what it already did.

choices: Likely data exfiltration or unauthorized tooling on a server — isolate for investigation and check what was sent
Normal admin activity — curl is a standard tool
A vendor API change — update the allowlist to include the file-sharing site
A logging error — servers cannot run curl

10.4.0.21 - - [03/Oct/2026:03:12:44] "POST https://files.example-share.net/upload" "curl/7.68.0" 200 1843200
scenarios.hint: Forget the tool for a second — what did you expect this server to talk to, and what did it actually do?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most defensible conclusion and action?
scenarios.situation: Proxy logs show a server in the DMZ — which should only talk to two vendor APIs — making HTTPS requests to a file-sharing site with a user-agent of 'curl/7.68.0'.
scenarios.title: The odd user-agent
scenarios.why: A DMZ server violating its known-good communication profile (new destination + interactive tooling user-agent + large POST) is exactly what allowlist-style monitoring is for. curl itself is legitimate, but context makes it suspicious. Isolate, determine what the 1.8 MB upload contained, and check how curl got invoked on that box.

choices: The attacker manipulated the logs — treat all timestamps as hostile
Clock skew between sources (NTP misconfiguration) — normalize to a common reference before building the timeline
The SIEM is parsing timezones incorrectly — reindex everything
Log sources always disagree; pick the firewall as authoritative
evidence: Review the relevant log-analysis documentation.
scenarios.hint: If the clocks disagree, can you trust the order of events? What single service prevents this?
scenarios.prompt: What is the root issue and the fix?
scenarios.situation: You are correlating firewall, proxy, and endpoint logs for an incident, but the timestamps disagree by up to 9 minutes across sources. The firewall shows the connection before the endpoint shows the process launch.
scenarios.title: The clock problem
scenarios.why: Correlating across sources requires synchronized clocks; even minutes of NTP drift invert cause and effect in a timeline. Normalize timestamps to one reference (usually UTC from a reliable source) and note the skew. Fix the systemic issue by enforcing NTP everywhere — timeline integrity is a prerequisite for sound conclusions.

choices: Nothing — no logs means no malicious activity on that server
Treat the log gap as a detection blind spot: investigate why the forwarder stopped, backfill if possible, and create a 'log source heartbeat' alert
Restart the SIEM to force the logs through
Assume the server was decommissioned and remove it from monitoring
evidence: Review the relevant log-analysis documentation.
scenarios.hint: A green dashboard with a blind spot — who benefits most from that silence?
scenarios.prompt: What is the priority action?
scenarios.situation: Your SIEM dashboard is green, but you notice one critical file server has sent zero logs for 6 days. No alert fired for the gap.
scenarios.title: The silent sensor
scenarios.why: Absence of logs is itself a signal — attackers disable logging to work unseen, and forwarders die quietly on their own too. Every log source needs a heartbeat/dead-man alert. Investigate the forwarder, determine whether the gap was malicious or mechanical, and make sure the gap can never go unnoticed again.

scenarios.title: Log Analysis: Production Incident
scenarios.situation: A production Log Analysis system is experiencing degraded performance. Users are affected. You need to diagnose and resolve quickly without making things worse.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response sequence for this Log Analysis degradation?
choices: Assess impact and declare incident severity, check recent changes (deployments, config changes), review key metrics to isolate the layer, implement the least-risky mitigation first, verify recovery, then conduct a blameless post-mortem.
Immediately restart all Log Analysis components — fastest way to resolve.
Roll back the last deployment without investigation — it's always the deployment.
Wait and monitor — it might resolve itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Incident response follows: (1) Assess impact (how bad? who's affected?), (2) Check recent changes (what changed?), (3) Isolate via metrics (which layer?), (4) Mitigate with least risk (don't make it worse), (5) Verify recovery, (6) Post-mortem (prevent recurrence). Skipping steps in Log Analysis incidents causes extended outages.
scenarios.hint: Remember the incident response phases from the lessons. What's the order?
evidence: Review Log Analysis requirements and constraints.

choices: Alert on every powershell.exe execution to catch everything
Alert on powershell.exe with command lines containing -EncodedCommand or -enc, excluding known-good admin automation by path/hash
Alert only when the username is 'administrator'
Block PowerShell at the EDR level instead of detecting
evidence: Review the relevant detection-engineering documentation.
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes the attacker's PowerShell from the admin's — the binary name, or something about how it was invoked?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a good first version of this detection?
scenarios.situation: After the encoded-PowerShell incident, you are asked to write a detection so the next occurrence fires automatically. The team uses Sigma-style generic rules converted to the SIEM.
scenarios.title: Writing the rule
scenarios.why: Good detections balance fidelity and coverage: target the malicious behavior (encoded command lines), not the tool itself (PowerShell is used legitimately everywhere). Exclusions for known-good automation keep the signal usable. 'Alert on everything' creates alert fatigue, which is how real attacks get missed.

choices: No flaw — new external IPs from servers are always malicious
Servers legitimately contact CDNs, update mirrors, and vendor APIs; without a learned baseline of normal destinations, the rule will drown the SOC in false positives
The flaw is the SIEM can't track new IPs — use the firewall instead
Only alert on weekends when admins aren't working
evidence: Review the relevant detection-engineering documentation.
scenarios.hint: How many legitimate external connections does a patched, updating server make in a day?
scenarios.prompt: What is the flaw, and what should come first?
scenarios.situation: You want a detection for 'unusual outbound connections from servers.' A colleague suggests alerting on any server connecting to a new external IP.
scenarios.title: Baseline before alert
scenarios.why: Anomaly detection without a baseline is just noise generation. Servers have legitimate, dynamic external dependencies (patch mirrors, CDNs, SaaS APIs). The engineering work is building the baseline first — known-good destinations per server role — then alerting on deviation. Otherwise analysts tune out, and the rule's true-positive gets buried.

choices: The team needs more threat intel feeds with more hashes
Detections sit at the bottom of the pyramid (trivial for attackers to change); move up toward TTPs and behaviors that are painful to change
Hashes are the most reliable indicator — the problem is analyst speed
Stop writing detections and rely on the EDR vendor's defaults
evidence: Review the relevant detection-engineering documentation.
scenarios.hint: What costs the attacker more: registering a new domain, or rewriting their entire intrusion methodology?
scenarios.prompt: Using the Pyramid of Pain concept, what is the diagnosis and remedy?
scenarios.situation: Your detections mostly fire on file hashes and malicious IPs. After each incident, the attacker changes hashes and infrastructure and returns undetected.
scenarios.title: What level are we detecting?
scenarios.why: The Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it costs the adversary to change them: hashes and IPs are cheap to rotate; TTPs (techniques like encoded PowerShell from Office apps, credential dumping patterns) force real re-engineering. Climbing the pyramid is the core of mature detection engineering — behavior-based detections survive infrastructure churn.

choices: Delete the rule — it's useless
Tune it: exclude the backup process by path/signer, keep the behavior detection for everything else, and document the exclusion
Tell analysts to read every alert more carefully
Lower the threshold so it fires even more and nobody can ignore it
evidence: Review the relevant detection-engineering documentation.
scenarios.hint: The rule isn't wrong about the behavior — it's wrong about the scope. What narrows scope without losing coverage?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct engineering response?
scenarios.situation: A detection for 'mass file modification' fires 300 times a day, all from the backup software. Analysts now bulk-close it without reading.
scenarios.title: The noisy rule
scenarios.why: Noisy rules train analysts to ignore the queue — that is how breaches hide. Tuning (scoped exclusions for known-good software, documented and reviewed) preserves the detection's value while restoring trust in the alert. Deleting it surrenders the coverage; scolding analysts ignores the engineering failure.

choices: Wait for a real attacker to test it in production
Run a safe, controlled atomic test (e.g., a benign tool exercising the same API pattern in an isolated lab) and confirm the full pipeline from event to alert
Point to the vendor documentation saying the logic is sound
Assume it works because the query syntax is valid
evidence: Review the relevant detection-engineering documentation.
scenarios.hint: What breaks between 'the query is correct' and 'the analyst gets paged'?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right validation approach?
scenarios.situation: You shipped a new detection for credential dumping via LSASS access. Leadership asks: 'How do you know it actually fires?'
scenarios.title: Prove the rule works
scenarios.why: An untested detection is a hope, not a control. Atomic testing — safely reproducing the behavior in a lab and verifying the event flows through collection, parsing, rule logic, and alerting — proves the whole pipeline. Syntax validity proves nothing about field mapping, log source coverage, or alert routing.

choices: Only on the initial VPN brute force — stop them at the door
Across multiple stages, with emphasis on the chokepoints the attacker cannot skip: discovery patterns and recovery-disabling commands
Only on the encryption stage — it's the most visible
Nowhere — ransomware affiliates change playbooks too fast
evidence: Review the relevant detection-engineering documentation.
scenarios.hint: Which steps in that playbook are optional for the attacker, and which are mandatory?
scenarios.prompt: Where should detection engineering focus for the most defensive value?
scenarios.situation: Threat intel reports a ransomware affiliate's playbook: initial access via VPN brute force → discovery with built-in tools → disabling recovery → mass encryption.
scenarios.title: Detection from the kill chain
scenarios.why: Defense in depth for detections: cover multiple kill-chain stages, but weight the stages the adversary cannot skip. Every ransomware operator must do discovery and must neutralize recovery — those behaviors are stable across affiliates. Initial access varies; encryption is too late. Chokepoint detections give the earliest reliable warning.

scenarios.title: Detection Engineering: Code Review Finding
scenarios.situation: During code review, you notice a Detection Engineering implementation that works but has potential issues. The author is a junior developer who is eager to merge.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle this Detection Engineering code review as a senior team member?
choices: Provide specific, actionable feedback: explain the issue, why it matters, suggest a concrete fix, and offer to pair on the solution. Approve the approach but request changes on the implementation.
Approve immediately — it works, and you don't want to discourage the junior.
Reject outright with 'this is wrong' — they'll figure it out.
Rewrite the code yourself — faster than explaining.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Effective code review for Detection Engineering: (1) Be specific about the issue (not 'this is bad'), (2) Explain the impact (why it matters), (3) Suggest a fix (don't just criticize), (4) Offer help (mentorship). This builds both better Detection Engineering code and better engineers.
scenarios.hint: Think about the goal of code review — it's not just gatekeeping, it's team growth.
evidence: Review Detection Engineering requirements and constraints.

choices: Both are P1 — all malware and all anomalous logins are critical
A is low (contained, low-value asset, automated response worked); B is high (privileged account, crown-jewel system, odd hour) and needs immediate investigation
A is critical (malware!) and B is low (logins happen all the time)
Severity doesn't matter as long as both get tickets
evidence: Review the relevant triage-escalation documentation.
scenarios.hint: Which of these two, if real, costs the organization more — and which one is already contained?
scenarios.prompt: How should severity be assigned?
scenarios.situation: Two alerts arrive together: (A) malware signature hit on a single kiosk PC in the lobby, auto-quarantined; (B) a service account logging into the backup server from an unusual location at 3 AM.
scenarios.title: What severity is this?
scenarios.why: Severity is a function of asset value, blast radius, containment state, and attacker advantage — not of how scary the alert name sounds. A quarantined kiosk is a cleanup task; a privileged account touching backups at 3 AM threatens the organization's ability to recover. Triage calibrates response effort to actual risk.

choices: True positive — a scan really happened, so the detection worked
False positive — no scan happened
Benign positive: the activity is real but authorized; document it and tune the detection to exclude the scanner
Escalate as an insider threat — scanning is never allowed
evidence: Review the relevant triage-escalation documentation.
scenarios.hint: Did the sensor lie? Was the activity malicious? Those are two different questions.
scenarios.prompt: How should this be dispositioned?
scenarios.situation: An alert fires: 'Suspicious: nmap scan detected from internal host.' Investigation shows it is the vulnerability management team's scheduled scanner.
scenarios.title: True or false positive?
scenarios.why: This is the 'benign true positive' (real activity, authorized source). Calling it a true positive buries it with real threats; calling it a false positive misstates that the sensor worked correctly. The right move: document the authorized source and tune the detection (exclude the scanner's IP) so future alerts mean something.

choices: Handle alone until shift change — it's contained, so it's not urgent
Escalate now: confirmed malware of an unknown family on a corporate host meets escalation criteria even when contained, because scope is unverified
Delete the malware and close the ticket to keep MTTR low
Wait to see if more hosts get infected before deciding
evidence: Review the relevant triage-escalation documentation.
scenarios.hint: What do you actually know right now — and what is the most dangerous thing you don't know?
scenarios.prompt: Should you escalate to Tier 2 now, or handle and hand off at shift change?
scenarios.situation: It's 3 AM. You have a confirmed malware infection on one workstation, contained by EDR. No lateral movement seen yet, but the malware family is unknown.
scenarios.title: When to wake the lead
scenarios.why: Escalation criteria exist precisely for 'contained but unknown scope' — containment of one host does not prove the absence of others. Unknown malware family means unknown capabilities (wormable? credential theft?). Waking Tier 2 for scope verification is the job; waiting for more infections is how incidents become breaches.

choices: Nothing — Tier 2 can look it all up themselves
Host owner and role, process that made the connection, reputation/age of the destination, whether the destination appears in threat intel, and the surrounding timeline
A screenshot of the alert
The analyst's personal opinion about the user's trustworthiness
evidence: Review the relevant triage-escalation documentation.
scenarios.hint: What would Tier 2 look up in the first five minutes? Do that before escalating.
scenarios.prompt: What enrichment would make this escalation actionable?
scenarios.situation: You are about to escalate a suspicious outbound connection. Your draft note says: 'Host 10.2.4.15 connected to 198.51.100.9. Please advise.'
scenarios.title: Enrich before escalate
scenarios.why: An escalation without enrichment is a question, not a handoff — it forces Tier 2 to redo Tier 1's work. The five enrichments (who owns the host, what process, where it went, what intel says, what happened around it) let Tier 2 make a decision in minutes. Enrichment is the core value Tier 1 adds.

choices: Work each alert as a separate ticket to keep metrics accurate
Correlate them into a single incident — they are stages of one intrusion chain on one host
Close the phishing one as the root cause and ignore the rest
Escalate only the credential dump; it's the most severe
evidence: Review the relevant triage-escalation documentation.
scenarios.hint: Do these look like five coincidences, or five chapters of one story?
scenarios.prompt: How should these be handled?
scenarios.situation: Five alerts fired in 20 minutes: a phishing email, a macro execution, a C2 connection, a credential dump attempt, and data staging — all involving the same user and host.
scenarios.title: One incident or five?
scenarios.why: Alerts are observations; incidents are stories. Five alerts on one host in 20 minutes following the attack chain (phish → execution → C2 → creds → staging) is one intrusion, and splitting it across tickets fragments the response — nobody sees the full scope. Use EDR network isolation: it cuts attacker access while preserving remote forensic access and memory state
Shut the server down immediately to stop the encryption
Do nothing until Tier 3 confirms — containment needs senior approval

Force a password reset first, then monitor to see if the attacker comes back
Disable the account and consider the incident closed
Email the account owner and ask them to change their password
evidence: Review the relevant containment documentation.

scenarios.prompt: What is the correct containment sequence?

scenarios.title: The compromised account

Purge the message from all mailboxes via the security tools, block the URL/domain at gateway and proxy, and identify the 60 clickers for targeted follow-up
Shut down the mail server until the campaign passes
Only investigate the 60 clickers; the other 340 are fine

scenarios.prompt: What is the right containment approach?

scenarios.title: The phishing blast

Block only at DNS — one layer is enough
Don't block; keep watching indefinitely for intelligence
Block the IP but leave the domain resolvable
evidence: Review the relevant containment documentation.
scenarios.hint: What do you learn by watching for an hour — and what do you risk?
scenarios.prompt: What is the best practice for C2 blocking?

Reimaging before containment and evidence collection destroys forensic artifacts and may leave stolen credentials valid elsewhere
Reimaging is too expensive in analyst time
The user will lose their desktop wallpaper

scenarios.hint: The malware is on the disk, but where else might the attacker already be?

choices: Follow the playbook blindly — security overrides the business
Let the business decide — revenue comes first
Escalate to the incident commander with options and trade-offs (e.g., EDR isolation preserving DB function vs full isolation), so the risk decision is made explicitly at the right level
Quietly delay containment and hope the EDR handles it
evidence: Review the relevant containment documentation.

scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve the conflict?

scenarios.title: The server that can't go down

choices: All three are IOCs — they're all in the threat report
Hash and domain are IOCs (atomic, easily changed); WMI lateral movement and shadow-copy deletion are TTPs (behaviors, costly to change) — build lasting detections on the TTPs
All three are TTPs — anything describing the attacker is a TTP
The distinction doesn't matter operationally
evidence: Review the relevant threat-intel documentation.
scenarios.hint: Which of these can the attacker change in five minutes, and which would force them to rewrite their tools?
scenarios.prompt: Which items are IOCs and which are TTPs, and why does the distinction matter for your SOC?
scenarios.situation: A threat report lists: a SHA256 hash, a C2 domain, and 'uses WMI for lateral movement and disables Volume Shadow Copies before encryption.'
scenarios.title: IOC or TTP?
scenarios.why: IOCs are atomic artifacts the attacker rotates cheaply; TTPs are behaviors that require re-engineering to change. choices: More feeds — 40,000 IOCs is too few
Expiration and review: IOCs decay in value; stale indicators should age out or be re-validated, or the list becomes noise that slows enforcement
Blocking more aggressively to justify the list size
Deleting the whole list and starting over annually
evidence: Review the relevant threat-intel documentation.
scenarios.hint: What happens when a three-year-old 'malicious' domain gets bought by a legitimate business?

scenarios.title: Stale intel

choices: Pick the more likely actor — the board needs an answer
Report what is known with confidence levels, note the conflicting evidence, and explain that premature attribution can misdirect the response
Refuse to discuss attribution — it's never the SOC's job
Attribute based on the malware language strings alone

scenarios.hint: What changes about your containment plan if the attribution is wrong?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct analyst response?

choices: It's just documentation overhead — the report is readable as-is

ATT&CK mapping is only useful for red teams
Mapping replaces the need to read the report
evidence: Review the relevant threat-intel documentation.
scenarios.hint: How do you answer 'are we covered against this report' without a common map?

choices: More feeds — three is not enough for coverage
Intelligence requirements: defined questions from stakeholders (what do we need to know to defend?) that direct collection and measure the feeds' value
Cheaper feeds — cost is the only problem
Nothing — reading reports is the purpose of intel
evidence: Review the relevant threat-intel documentation.
scenarios.hint: If you can't name the question a feed answers, how do you know it's worth paying for?
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, per intelligence best practice?
scenarios.situation: Your team subscribes to three expensive intel feeds. When asked what decisions they drive, the answer is 'we read the reports.'
scenarios.title: Intel with a purpose
scenarios.why: Intelligence without requirements is just news. The intel cycle starts with direction: stakeholder questions ('which ransomware groups target our sector?') that focus collection, processing, and dissemination — and let you evaluate whether a feed is worth its cost. choices: Share everything including internal hostnames and user data — speed helps everyone
Share sanitized indicators and TTPs through the ISAC (anonymized, no PII/internal identifiers), following your sharing policy and TLP markings
Share nothing — any sharing helps the attacker learn what you know
Post the full report publicly to warn everyone
evidence: Review the relevant threat-intel documentation.
scenarios.hint: What does the ISAC need to detect this — and what parts of your report would only help an attacker map your network?
scenarios.prompt: What is the responsible sharing posture?
scenarios.situation: You have finished investigating an intrusion with novel TTPs. A peer company in your sector ISAC asks for details. Legal is nervous.
scenarios.title: To share or not
scenarios.why: Collective defense works: the TTPs you share today become someone else's detection tomorrow, and vice versa. lessons.title: SOC Workflow — Core concepts
concepts: SOC tier structure: tier 1 owns monitoring, triage, initial evidence gathering, and playbook-driven containment, then escalates with complete notes. SOC continuity lives in handoff notes.
Tier 1 responsibilities: escalating with rich context is a feature of good Tier 1 work, not a failure.
Playbook discipline: disabling first is sometimes right, but only after the playbook's verification steps say so — context determines whether containment or clearance is next.
Shift handoff: a quick malicious-cause check (is the flapping consistent with an attack, or with hardware failure?) followed by a clean handoff to the NOC respects both missions.

lessons.title: Log Analysis — Core concepts
concepts: Auth log reading: every log source needs a heartbeat/dead-man alert.
DNS tunneling: high-entropy, unique subdomains at high volume to an unfamiliar domain is the textbook DNS tunneling/exfil pattern — data is encoded in the subdomain labels.

Malicious macro chain: winword spawning hidden, encoded PowerShell is one of the highest-fidelity malicious indicators in endpoint telemetry — it is the classic malicious-macro chain. Investigate the forwarder, determine whether the gap was malicious or mechanical, and make sure the gap can never go unnoticed again.
Apply Log Analysis — Core concepts principles systematically: understand the underlying model, follow established patterns, verify each step, and document decisions for maintainability.

Killing the process without understanding intent destroys evidence of what it already did.

lessons.title: Detection Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: Detection authoring: climbing the pyramid is the core of mature detection engineering — behavior-based detections survive infrastructure churn. Tuning (scoped exclusions for known-good software, documented and reviewed) preserves the detection's value while restoring trust in the alert.

Fidelity vs coverage: good detections balance fidelity and coverage: target the malicious behavior (encoded command lines), not the tool itself (PowerShell is used legitimately everywhere). Deleting it surrenders the coverage; scolding analysts ignores the engineering failure.

Pyramid of Pain: the Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it costs the adversary to change them: hashes and IPs are cheap to rotate; TTPs (techniques like encoded PowerShell from Office apps, credential dumping patterns) force real re-engineering.
TTP-based detection: anomaly detection without a baseline is just noise generation. An untested detection is a hope, not a control.

lessons.title: Triage & Escalation — Core concepts
concepts: Severity is a function of asset value, blast radius, containment state, and attacker advantage — not of how scary the alert name sounds.

Risk-based triage: triage calibrates response effort to actual risk. The professional move: finish the actual triage (one check), document honestly including the time pressure, and let the process record reflect reality.
Alert disposition: sLAs measure responsiveness, not correctness — closing an alert to beat the clock is metric gaming that can miss real threats.
Benign positives: this is the 'benign true positive' (real activity, authorized source).

Escalation criteria exist precisely for 'contained but unknown scope' — containment of one host does not prove the absence of others. An escalation without enrichment is a question, not a handoff — it forces Tier 2 to redo Tier 1's work.
Scope verification: waking Tier 2 for scope verification is the job; waiting for more infections is how incidents become breaches.

lessons.title: Containment — Core concepts
concepts: Host isolation: EDR isolation blocks network access (stopping spread and C2) while keeping the analyst's remote access for forensics and preserving volatile memory.

Evidence preservation: IR phases exist in order for a reason: contain (stop spread), then collect evidence, then eradicate, then recover. Pulling the cable or powering off destroys memory evidence and your ability to investigate remotely.

Account containment: containment must be complete and ordered: disable stops new auth, session/token revocation kills existing access (a password reset alone leaves stolen tokens valid), and only then does the hunt for attacker actions make sense.
Phishing containment: speed matters, but evidence-preserving containment is the trained response. Reset-without-revoke is the classic incomplete containment that lets the attacker stroll back in.

Mailbox purge removes the weapon from all 400 inboxes at once; gateway/proxy blocks neutralize the link even for anyone who kept a copy; the clicker list focuses the expensive human follow-up where risk actually materialized.

lessons.title: Threat Intel — Core concepts
concepts: IOCs are atomic artifacts the attacker rotates cheaply; TTPs are behaviors that require re-engineering to change. Hoarding IOCs is not defense; curated, fresh intel is.

Intel-driven detection: it also lets detections, intel, and adversary emulation all reference the same technique IDs — the foundation of a coherent detection program. Collective defense works: the TTPs you share today become someone else's detection tomorrow, and vice versa.

Intel lifecycle: a lifecycle — ingestion, validation, deployment, expiration/review — keeps intel operationally relevant. ATT&CK is the SOC's shared coordinate system: mapping intel to techniques lets you ask 'which of these can we detect today?' and turns a narrative report into a gap analysis.
Attribution with conflicting evidence is a confidence statement, not a guess.

Analytic confidence: the professional answer: 'consistent with, with moderate confidence, but conflicting evidence X means we cannot rule out Y' — and note that response actions don't depend on the flag the attacker flies.

lessons.title: SOC Analyst Operations — Core concepts
concepts: Triage by success and impact, not by volume: a single successful anomalous login outranks ten thousand failed attempts. Prioritization is the analyst's primary skill.
SIEM work is filter-aggregate-threshold: filter to the relevant events, aggregate by entity (user, IP, host), and apply a threshold. Most useful detections are built from this pattern.
Alert fatigue is fixed by tuning, not by ignoring or deleting: tighten logic, allowlist known-good behavior, and measure precision before and after.

Escalation has a threshold — active intrusion indicators (code execution, credential access attempts, lateral movement) trigger the IR playbook: isolate, preserve evidence, hand off. Blocked does not mean benign.
Threat intelligence decays: enrich indicators, respect first/last-seen dates, age out stale IoCs, and prefer durable TTP-based detections over ephemeral IPs and hashes.

example.code:
index=auth action=failure
| stats count by src_ip
| where count > 100
example.walkthrough: This Splunk-style query filters VPN/auth logs to failures, counts them per source IP, and keeps only sources above 100 — the classic brute-force hunt. Adapt the index name and threshold to your environment, and always sanity-check the results against known-good scanners before blocking.

pitfalls: Common trap: investigating alerts in arrival order instead of triaging by risk — FIFO is not a strategy.
Common trap: treating a blocked attack as a non-event — the attacker still achieved the steps before the block.
Common trap: blocking aged indicators without enrichment — stale IoCs generate false positives and erode trust in intel.
Common trap: writing detections with no threshold or aggregation — raw event counts are noise, not signal.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Soc Analyst move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.

lessons.title: How to Use This SOC Analyst Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: course overview, study strategy, key terminology) → Lessons (the deep-dives, in domain order) → Drills (practice scenarios, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on exercises) → Mock Assessment (timed simulation). Each layer assumes the one before. Skipping straight to the mock burns your one realistic practice run.

What 'SOC analyst' means in practice: this bootcamp prepares you for the real-world responsibilities of a SOC analyst, not just exam questions. Every lesson connects theory to the decisions you'll make on the job — what to check first, what to try next, how to explain your reasoning.

The SOC analyst interviews and operations strategy: (a) first pass — read every lesson in order without skipping, taking notes on concepts that feel unfamiliar; (b) second pass — work every scenario and lab, reading the 'why' explanations even for correct answers; (c) final pass — take the timed mock under realistic conditions (no pauses, no references).

How to read the scenarios: every scenario has a 'why' explanation — read it even when you got the answer right, because it explains the WRONG answers too (and real exams design wrong answers from those same misconceptions). The hint is there to unblock you, not to give away the answer.

Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key concepts out loud in your own words. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet — re-read that section.
Spaced repetition: revisit completed domains after 2-3 days. The bootcamp tracks your progress — use the dashboard to identify weak areas and drill those specifically before the mock.

example.code:
Week 1: Start Here + first 3 domains (lessons only)
Week 2: Remaining domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3: All labs + weak-area review
Week 4: Timed mock → review misses → targeted re-study
Exam/Interview: Confident and prepared
example.walkthrough: This 4-week plan assumes 1-2 hours per day. Adjust the pace to your schedule, but keep the order: lessons before scenarios, scenarios before labs, everything before the mock. The mock is a diagnostic tool — take it when you're ready to find gaps, not when you're still learning fundamentals.

pitfalls: Skipping the Start Here domain because 'I already know the basics' — the study strategy and terminology sections prevent wasted effort later.
Doing scenarios before reading the lessons — you'll memorize answers without understanding the concepts, and the mock will expose it.
Ignoring the 'why' explanations for correct answers — the wrong-answer analysis is where deep understanding comes from.
Taking the mock too early as a 'practice test' — it's a final validation, not a study tool. Use it once when ready.

lessons.title: SOC Analyst: Field Overview and Key Terminology
concepts: SOC Analyst sits at the intersection of theory and hands-on practice. The professionals who excel are those who can both explain the 'why' and execute the 'how' under pressure.

Key terminology is the price of admission — every domain in this bootcamp assumes you can use the core vocabulary precisely. When you encounter an unfamiliar term, stop and learn it before continuing.
The field rewards systems thinkers: people who see how components connect, not just isolated facts. The Systems Anatomy domain teaches this explicitly — start there after finishing Start Here.
Documentation is a professional skill, not an afterthought. As you learn, practice explaining concepts as if writing a runbook — clear, sequential, with the 'why' for each step.

example.code:
Weak answer: 'I know about X.'
Strong answer: 'X works by [mechanism]. In practice, I've used it to [application]. The key consideration is [tradeoff].'
example.walkthrough: This is the answer framework for interviews and exams: mechanism → application → tradeoff. Every lesson in this bootcamp is structured to build this three-part understanding. Practice using it from day one.

pitfalls: Using jargon without understanding — interviewers will probe deeper, and vague terminology collapses under follow-up questions.
Learning tools before concepts — tools change, but the underlying principles persist across versions and vendors.
Neglecting the 'boring' fundamentals — advanced topics assume solid foundations, and gaps there compound.

lessons.title: Study Strategy: From Learning to Mastery
concepts: The learning pyramid: reading alone retains ~10%, but teaching someone else retains ~90%. After each domain, explain the concepts to an imaginary colleague — or better, a real one.
Deliberate practice: don't just re-read weak areas, actively test yourself on them. The scenario drills are designed for this — they force retrieval, not recognition.
Error analysis: every wrong answer is data. Log your misses by domain and concept. Patterns in your errors reveal exactly where to focus.
The 80/20 rule: 80% of exam/interview questions come from 20% of the material — the core concepts that everything else builds on. This bootcamp front-loads those in the early domains.
Sleep consolidates learning: study sessions followed by sleep outperform cramming. Don't sacrifice rest for extra hours — your brain needs downtime to build connections.

example.code:
Study session template (60 min):
  0-10:  Review previous session's key concepts (retrieval)
  10-40: New lesson + scenario practice (learning)
  40-50: Lab exercise (application)
  50-60: Write summary notes (consolidation)

End each session by writing tomorrow's starting point.
example.walkthrough: This template prevents the two biggest study failures: passive re-reading (no retrieval) and marathon sessions (diminishing returns). The 10-minute review at the start compounds over weeks — by exam day, early material is rock solid.

pitfalls: Cramming the night before — it produces familiarity (recognition) without recall ability, which is what exams test.
Studying only strengths because it feels good — the discomfort of weak areas is where growth happens.
No error log — without tracking misses, you repeat the same mistakes and can't measure improvement.
Isolation — discussing concepts with others (or writing about them) exposes gaps that solo study hides.
lessons.try_it: Create your error log now — a simple document with columns for date, domain, concept missed, and correct understanding. You'll use this throughout.

lessons.title: What Success Looks Like: Exam and Interview Readiness
concepts: Readiness isn't a feeling — it's measurable. You're ready when: (a) mock scores are consistently above the passing threshold, (b) you can explain any lesson's key concepts without notes, (c) scenario misses are rare and random (not clustered in one domain).
For exams: time management is a skill to practice. The mock simulates real timing — use it to calibrate your pace (e.g., if the exam allows 2 minutes per question, practice at that pace).
For interviews: prepare stories, not just answers. 'Tell me about a time when...' needs specific examples. As you work labs, note what you built and what went wrong — these become interview stories.
The night before: no new material. Review your error log, skim key concept summaries, and rest. Confidence comes from preparation, not last-minute cramming.
A SOC analyst is expected to handle ambiguity. Exams and interviews test this with incomplete scenarios — practice making reasonable assumptions and stating them explicitly.

example.code:
Readiness checklist:
  [ ] All lessons completed with passing knowledge checks
  [ ] All scenarios attempted, error log reviewed
  [ ] All labs completed successfully
  [ ] Mock score above target (with time to spare)
  [ ] Can whiteboard core concepts from memory
  [ ] Error patterns addressed (no clustered weaknesses)
example.walkthrough: Go through this checklist honestly one week before your target date. Any unchecked item is a priority. If multiple items are unchecked, consider adjusting your timeline — rushing into an exam unprepared wastes time and money.

pitfalls: Confusing completion with mastery — finishing all lessons doesn't mean you're ready; the mock score is the real indicator.
Ignoring time pressure in practice — untimed perfection doesn't transfer to timed exams.
No interview stories prepared — technical knowledge without communication skills underperforms in interviews.

lessons.title: Capstone Project: Build Your SOC Analyst Portfolio Piece
concepts: A portfolio project proves you can DO the work, not just answer questions about it. Employers and interviewers remember what you built far longer than what you scored.
Choose a project that demonstrates the full lifecycle: planning → implementation → testing → documentation → presentation. A SOC analyst is expected to own work end-to-end.
Scope ruthlessly: a small project done well beats an ambitious project done poorly. Pick something you can complete in 2-4 weekends.
Document as you build, not after. Future-you (and interviewers) need to understand your decisions, not just your results.
Make it visible: GitHub repository with a professional README, architecture diagram, and demo instructions. If it's not on GitHub, it didn't happen.

example.code:
Project structure:
  README.md          # What, why, how to run
  docs/
    architecture.md  # System design and decisions
    setup.md         # Step-by-step build guide
  src/               # Your implementation
  tests/             # Validation that it works
  demo/              # Screenshots or video walkthrough
example.walkthrough: This structure signals professionalism. The README is your first impression — write it for someone who's never seen the project. The architecture doc shows you think before you build. Tests prove it works. Start with the README (write what you'll build), then implement.

pitfalls: Tutorial hell — following a guide step-by-step without understanding teaches nothing. Build something original, even if small.
No documentation — undocumented code is unusable code, and interviewers will ask you to explain your decisions.
Perfectionism paralysis — ship a working v1, then iterate. A deployed simple project beats an unreleased complex one.
Skipping the 'why' — every technical choice needs a reason. 'I used X because...' is an interview question waiting to happen.

lessons.title: Presenting Your Work: From Build to Interview Story
concepts: The STAR method for technical stories: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what you did, specifically) → Result (measurable outcome).
Lead with the problem, not the technology. 'We needed to automate X because manual process took Y hours' is more compelling than 'I used tool Z.'
Quantify everything: time saved, errors reduced, performance improved, users served. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.
Prepare for deep dives: interviewers will pick one detail and probe. Know your architecture cold — every component, every tradeoff, every alternative you considered.
Show the messy parts: what went wrong, how you debugged it, what you'd do differently. This demonstrates maturity more than a flawless narrative.

example.code:
Weak: 'I built a thing with React.'
Strong: 'Our team spent 6 hours weekly on manual deployments. I built an automated pipeline using [tools] that cut deployment time to 15 minutes and eliminated config drift. The hardest part was [challenge] — I solved it by [approach].'
example.walkthrough: Notice the structure: problem (6 hours wasted) → action (built pipeline) → result (15 min, no drift) → depth (hardest part + solution). Practice telling your capstone story in 2 minutes, then be ready to go deep on any part.

pitfalls: Vague claims without specifics — 'I improved performance' means nothing; 'I reduced load time from 4s to 800ms by...' is compelling.
Only preparing the happy path — interviewers specifically ask about failures and challenges.
Memorizing a script — stories should feel conversational, not rehearsed. Know the beats, not the words.
No demo ready — always have a live demo, screenshots, or video. 'Let me show you' beats 'trust me.'

lessons.title: Beyond the Capstone: Continuous Growth
concepts: The capstone is a starting point, not a finish line. The best SOC analysts are continuous learners — the field evolves, and so should you.
Build in public: share your learnings (blog posts, conference talks, open source contributions). Teaching solidifies your knowledge and builds your professional reputation.
Find your niche: general competence gets you hired, but deep expertise in a specific area makes you indispensable. Use the capstone to explore what energizes you.
Mentor others: explaining concepts to junior colleagues is the fastest way to deepen your own understanding and develop leadership skills.
Stay current: follow key practitioners, read release notes, experiment with new tools in a lab. Allocate 2-3 hours weekly to deliberate learning.

example.code:
Growth plan template:
  Monthly: One deep-dive (new tool, advanced concept)
  Quarterly: One shareable output (blog, talk, contribution)
  Annually: One significant skill addition (certification, major project)

  Track: What did I learn? What did I build? What did I teach?
example.walkthrough: This isn't about hustle culture — it's about intentional growth. The monthly deep-dive keeps you sharp, the quarterly output builds your portfolio, the annual skill prevents stagnation. Adjust the pace to your life, but keep the habit.

pitfalls: Stopping after the capstone — skills atrophy without use. Keep building, even small things.
Learning without applying — knowledge without practice fades quickly. Always pair learning with doing.
No community — solo learning is slower and lonelier. Find peers, join groups, contribute.

lessons.title: Query Optimization
concepts: Filter early: time bounds and index filters first — reduces data scanned
Use specific fields, not full text search — _index and sourcetype filters are fastest
Stats before sort: aggregate then sort the smaller result set
Subsearches are expensive — use joins or lookups where possible

example.code:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 earliest=-24h
| stats count by TargetUserName, IpAddress
| where count > 10
| sort -count
example.walkthrough: This finds brute force attempts: filter to failed logons first (small dataset), then aggregate. The time bound is critical — without it, you scan all history.

pitfalls: No time bounds — queries scan everything, timeout or cost fortune
Full text search — slow; use field extractions
Sorting before aggregating — sorts millions of rows instead of hundreds
lessons.try_it: Optimize a slow query in your SIEM. Measure before/after execution time and data scanned.

lessons.title: Static Analysis Basics
concepts: Hashes first: MD5/SHA256 → VirusTotal, check prevalence — known malware is quickly identified
Strings reveal: URLs, IPs, registry keys, commands — the malware's intentions in plaintext
PE headers show: compile time, imports (what APIs it uses), sections (packed?)
Never execute on your workstation — use isolated sandbox or VM

example.code:
Triage workflow:
  1. Hash → VirusTotal (known? what family?)
  2. Strings → URLs, IPs, interesting text

lessons.title: Wireshark for Analysts
concepts: Filter first: ip.addr == X, http, dns — reduce noise before analyzing

example.code:
C2 detection in PCAP:
  1. Statistics → Conversations: sort by bytes — beaconing stands out
  2. Filter: dns — look for long, random-looking domains (DGA)
  3. Follow TCP stream on suspicious connection
  4. Check: regular intervals? Small packets? Encrypted?
  5. Extract: any downloaded payloads via Export Objects
example.walkthrough: Beaconing is periodic — the IO Graph shows regular spikes. Human traffic is bursty and irregular.

pitfalls: No capture filters — full packet capture fills disks; filter at capture time
Ignoring DNS — C2 often starts with DNS; it's high-value, low-volume

lessons.title: SOC Workflow: Performance Optimization and Scaling
concepts: Measure first, optimize second: profile SOC Workflow operations to find actual bottlenecks, not assumed ones.

Scale horizontally when possible: stateless SOC Workflow components scale linearly; stateful ones need careful design.

Optimization workflow:
  1. Baseline: Measure current performance (p50, p95, p99)
  2. Profile: Identify the bottleneck (CPU? I/O? Network?)
  3. Hypothesize: What's the root cause?
  4. Optimize: Change one thing
  5. Measure: Did it improve? By how much?
  6. Repeat or revert
example.walkthrough: Follow this workflow for a real SOC Workflow performance issue. Document the baseline, the change, and the measured improvement. If the change didn't help, revert it — don't accumulate complexity without benefit.

pitfalls: Optimizing without measuring — you can't improve what you don't measure.
Premature optimization — clean code first, fast code when profiling shows it's needed.
Ignoring the 99th percentile — averages hide the worst user experiences.

sections.heading: SOC Workflow
items: SOC tier structure — tier 1 owns monitoring, triage, initial evidence gathering, and playbook-driven containment, then escalates with complete notes. SOC continuity lives in handoff notes.
Tier 1 responsibilities — escalating with rich context is a feature of good Tier 1 work, not a failure.
Playbook discipline — disabling first is sometimes right, but only after the playbook's verification steps say so — context determines whether containment or clearance is next.
Shift handoff — a quick malicious-cause check (is the flapping consistent with an attack, or with hardware failure?) followed by a clean handoff to the NOC respects both missions.
Common trap — close the ticket so the queue looks clean; the next shift will see the isolated host.
Common trap — the SOC is more efficient; the metric proves the team improved.
Common trap — playbooks are only used after an incident is declared closed.
Common trap — hardware failures are never the SOC's problem.

items: Detection authoring — climbing the pyramid is the core of mature detection engineering — behavior-based detections survive infrastructure churn. Tuning (scoped exclusions for known-good software, documented and reviewed) preserves the detection's value while restoring trust in t…

Fidelity vs coverage — good detections balance fidelity and coverage: target the malicious behavior (encoded command lines), not the tool itself (PowerShell is used legitimately everywhere). Deleting it surrenders the coverage; scolding analysts ignores the engineering failure.

Pyramid of Pain — the Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how much it costs the adversary to change them: hashes and IPs are cheap to rotate; TTPs (techniques like encoded PowerShell from Office apps, credential dumping patterns) force real re-engineering.
TTP-based detection — anomaly detection without a baseline is just noise generation. An untested detection is a hope, not a control.
Common trap — alert on every powershell.exe execution to catch everything.

Common trap — stop writing detections and rely on the EDR vendor's defaults.

sections.heading: Triage & Escalation
items: Severity — is a function of asset value, blast radius, containment state, and attacker advantage — not of how scary the alert name sounds.

Risk-based triage — triage calibrates response effort to actual risk. The professional move: finish the actual triage (one check), document honestly including the time pressure, and let the process record reflect reality.
Alert disposition — sLAs measure responsiveness, not correctness — closing an alert to beat the clock is metric gaming that can miss real threats.
Benign positives — this is the 'benign true positive' (real activity, authorized source).

Escalation criteria exist precisely for 'contained but unknown scope' — containment of one host does not prove the absence of others. An escalation without enrichment is a question, not a handoff — it forces Tier 2 to redo Tier 1's work.
Scope verification — waking Tier 2 for scope verification is the job; waiting for more infections is how incidents become breaches.
Common trap — work each alert as a separate ticket to keep metrics accurate.
Common trap — severity doesn't matter as long as both get tickets.
Common trap — let the SLA breach; accuracy matters more than the clock.
Common trap — escalate it solely to reset the SLA timer.

sections.heading: Containment
items: Host isolation — EDR isolation blocks network access (stopping spread and C2) while keeping the analyst's remote access for forensics and preserving volatile memory.

Evidence preservation — IR phases exist in order for a reason: contain (stop spread), then collect evidence, then eradicate, then recover. Pulling the cable or powering off destroys memory evidence and your ability to investigate remotely.

Account containment — containment must be complete and ordered: disable stops new auth, session/token revocation kills existing access (a password reset alone leaves stolen tokens valid), and only then does the hunt for attacker actions make sense.
Phishing containment — speed matters, but evidence-preserving containment is the trained response. Reset-without-revoke is the classic incomplete containment that lets the attacker stroll back in.

Mailbox — Mailbox purge removes the weapon from all 400 inboxes at once; gateway/proxy blocks neutralize the link even for anyone who kept a copy; the clicker list focuses the expensive human follow-up where risk actually materialized.
Common trap — disable the account and consider the incident closed.
Common trap — email the account owner and ask them to change their password.
Common trap — quietly delay containment and hope the EDR handles it.
Common trap — physical disconnection is the fastest, most certain isolation.

Intel-driven detection — it also lets detections, intel, and adversary emulation all reference the same technique IDs — the foundation of a coherent detection program. Collective defense works: the TTPs you share today become someone else's detection tomorrow, and vice versa.

Analytic confidence — the professional answer: 'consistent with, with moderate confidence, but conflicting evidence X means we cannot rule out Y' — and note that response actions don't depend on the flag the attacker flies.

Common trap — mapping replaces the need to read the report.
Common trap — any sharing helps the attacker learn what you know.
